name: Seep Worm
description:
The Seep Worm is not technically a worm, though it resembles one. It descends from slender glass eels — juvenile European eel — that entered GLMZ's drainage infrastructure through lake intake systems and never completed their metamorphosis to adult form. Over generations of living in the dark and in chemically disrupted water that likely interferes with the hormonal triggers for metamorphosis, a population has permanently neotenic, remaining in juvenile form and reproducing in that state. The result is a creature that looks like a white thread, ten to forty centimeters long, nearly transparent, moving with the slow glass-eel undulation through sediment and biofilm layers in drainage pipe walls.

Seep Worms live in the biofilm and sediment layer itself rather than open water — they are semi-infaunal, pushing through wet sediment and the thick microbial mats that coat drainage infrastructure walls. They feed entirely on bacteria, fungi, and organic particulate, effectively being detritivores at the base of the tunnel food web. They lack meaningful electroreception — their sensory suite is primarily chemoreception, following chemical gradients through sediment. Their populations can be enormous without being visible: a single pipe section may contain thousands of individuals living in the wall layer, entirely invisible unless the biofilm is disturbed and they pour out into the water column in pale drifting clouds.

Seep Worms are significant ecologically because they form the nutritional base that supports the entire tunnel food chain — Drain Eels, Conduit Lampreys, Bile Knifefish all feed on the clouds of pale bodies when biofilm is disturbed. Their presence indicates a functioning tunnel ecosystem. They are almost never individually noticed by people, but their mass emergence events — triggered by pressure changes, chemical shocks, or physical disturbance of biofilm walls — are the origin of reports of 'white water' in certain drainage sections, or the phenomenon workers describe as a pipe 'bleeding pale.' These events are harmless but deeply unpleasant to witness.
diet: Bacteria, fungi, organic particulate in biofilm and sediment
notable_traits: Permanent neotenic form — juvenile eel that reproduces without metamorphosing
Semi-infaunal lifestyle within biofilm and sediment layers
Mass emergence in pale clouds when biofilm is disturbed
Ecological keystone — base of tunnel food web
encounters: Almost never encountered as individuals. Mass emergence events produce clouds of pale drifting threads in disturbed pipe sections — visible to workers during high-pressure cleaning operations or after chemical shocks. The 'white water' or 'bleeding pale' reports are Seep Worm emergences.
known_uses: Significant research interest from bioremediation researchers — their gut microbiome processes an unusual range of industrial contaminants. Helix Biosystems has funded at least two studies. Also used as live feed in some aquatic chimera households that maintain drainage fauna.
story_hooks: A high-pressure drain cleaning operation in a contested subsector caused a mass Seep Worm emergence that flowed into a Tier 2 district's ornamental canal system — now white threads are drifting through what was a premium amenity space, and the development company wants answers and someone to blame.

Helix Biosystems' bioremediation research on Seep Worm gut microbiomes has been producing unexpected results — the worms in a specific drainage section are processing a compound that shouldn't exist in GLMZ's chemical profile. Something is being disposed of down there that isn't on any permit.
